prompt: Design a service that lets neighbours lend physical books. Prevent two borrowers reserving the same copy; support waiting lists, late returns, and unreliable notifications.
provenance: Original synthetic answer authored for mockr; not an actual candidate or human-scored label.

transcript.answer: Support catalog search, per-copy holds, returns, FIFO waitlists and asynchronous alerts. Non-goals are payments and shipping. Reservation correctness takes priority over availability; target p95 reads below 300 ms.

With 50000 members and three catalog reads daily, average reads are 1.74 per second; at 50x peak about 87. If each creates 12 reservations yearly, 600000 records at 1 KB use about 600 MB yearly before indexes and replicas.

POST /copies/{copy_id}/holds requires a client idempotency key, authenticated member and expiry policy. A reused key returns the original hold. Conflicts return 409. GET /holds/{id} provides status; cancellation is idempotent.

Titles and physical copies are separate. Holds reference a copy and member, with state and expiry timestamps. A partial unique constraint protects active holds. A transaction locks the copy while claiming or expiring a hold; waitlist entries have monotonic sequence ids.

An outbox row commits with the hold. Workers deliver notifications with deduplication and backoff; failed alerts never undo a reservation. Index catalog queries, cache public metadata and monitor lock wait, p95 latency, waitlist age and replica lag.

Postgres transactions simplify unique ownership. Eventual consistency works for catalog indexing but not concurrent claims. Sharding by neighborhood could isolate local demand but complicates cross-neighborhood waits. I would measure lock contention before adding that complexity.
